subject: physics

items.q: Which statement best describes the internal energy of a system?
items.correct: The energy stored inside the system by its own particles
items.misconception: The temperature the system reaches when it is heated
items.why: Temperature is the only number students routinely attach to a hot object, and 'hot' and 'full of energy' are used interchangeably in everyday speech. Temperature is linked to the average kinetic energy of the particles. Internal energy is the total for all of them, so it depends on how many particles there are as well as how fast they move.
items.random_wrong: The heat that flowed in and is now held inside

items.q: Internal energy is the total of which two energy stores of the particles in a system?
items.correct: The kinetic energy and the potential energy of the particles
items.misconception: The kinetic energy of every one of the particles, only
items.why: Particle animations and models show particles moving, but nothing on screen represents the energy stored in the forces between them. Particles also attract one another, so energy is stored in their positions. That potential energy is part of internal energy and is the part that changes during melting and boiling.
items.random_wrong: The chemical energy and the thermal energy of all the particles

items.q: Where does the potential energy part of a system's internal energy come from?
items.correct: From the positions of particles and the forces between them
items.misconception: From the speeds at which the particles are moving about inside
items.why: Particle animations and models show particles moving, but nothing on screen represents the energy stored in the forces between them. Particles also attract one another, so energy is stored in their positions. That potential energy is part of internal energy and is the part that changes during melting and boiling.
items.random_wrong: From the height of the system above the floor of the laboratory

items.q: Heating a system increases the energy of the particles that make it up. Which pair of outcomes does the specification give for this?
items.correct: It raises the temperature or it produces a change of state
items.misconception: It always raises the temperature of the system, without exception
items.why: Almost every everyday example of heating (a kettle, an oven, a radiator) does raise a temperature, so the exception is never met. Heating increases the energy of the particles. That either raises the temperature of the system or produces a change of state, not always the former.
items.random_wrong: It raises the temperature and it always changes state as well

items.q: A beaker of ice at 0 °C is heated steadily by an immersion heater until all the ice has melted. What does the heating do during that time?
items.correct: It increases the energy stored and produces a change of state
items.misconception: It raises the temperature of the ice steadily as it melts
items.why: Almost every everyday example of heating (a kettle, an oven, a radiator) does raise a temperature, so the exception is never met. Heating increases the energy of the particles. That either raises the temperature of the system or produces a change of state, not always the former.
items.random_wrong: The energy stored stays the same as the temperature holds steady

items.q: When a substance is heated and its temperature increases, the size of that increase depends on which three things?
items.correct: The mass, the type of material and the energy input to it
items.misconception: The mass, the final temperature and the energy supplied
items.why: The final reading is the number the thermometer shows at the end, and the symbol ∆ is skimmed over rather than read as 'change in'. ∆ means 'change in'. Subtract the starting temperature from the final temperature before substituting.
items.random_wrong: The volume, the type of material and the total time of heating

items.q: 1 kg of water and 1 kg of cooking oil are each supplied with 20 000 J. The oil ends up much hotter than the water. Why?
items.correct: Oil has a lower specific heat capacity than the water does
items.misconception: Equal masses given equal energy must reach equal temperatures
items.why: Students treat energy input as the only cause of a temperature rise and overlook the type of material, which is invisible in the numbers given. The increase in temperature depends on the mass, the type of material and the energy input. Two different materials respond differently to the same energy.
items.random_wrong: The oil has a much higher specific heat capacity than water

items.q: Which word equation for the change in thermal energy is the one given in the specification?
items.correct: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
items.misconception: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × the final temperature
items.why: The final reading is the number the thermometer shows at the end, and the symbol ∆ is skimmed over rather than read as 'change in'. ∆ means 'change in'. Subtract the starting temperature from the final temperature before substituting.
items.random_wrong: change in thermal energy = mass × specific latent heat × the temperature change

items.q: In the equation ∆E = m c ∆θ, what do the symbols c and ∆θ stand for?
items.correct: c is the specific heat capacity and ∆θ is the temperature change
items.misconception: c is the specific heat capacity and ∆θ is the final temperature
items.why: The final reading is the number the thermometer shows at the end, and the symbol ∆ is skimmed over rather than read as 'change in'. ∆ means 'change in'. Subtract the starting temperature from the final temperature before substituting.
items.random_wrong: c is the specific latent heat and ∆θ is the temperature change

items.q: In which of these situations does the equation ∆E = m c ∆θ apply?
items.correct: While the water in a kettle warms from 20 °C up to 90 °C
items.misconception: While ice at 0 °C melts into water that is also at 0 °C
items.why: Both are 'specific' properties, both are quoted per kilogram, and both appear in similar-looking equations. Use c and ∆E = m c ∆θ when the temperature changes; use L and E = m L when the state changes at constant temperature.
items.random_wrong: While water at 100 °C is boiling away steadily into steam

items.q: In ∆E = m c ∆θ, which units does the specification give for ∆E and for ∆θ?
items.correct: ∆E is in joules, J, and ∆θ is in degrees Celsius, °C
items.misconception: ∆E in joules, and ∆θ in joules per kilogram, J/kg
items.why: The 'per kilogram' part is remembered from the word 'specific' and the temperature condition is dropped. The definition fixes both conditions: one kilogram and one degree Celsius. So the unit carries both, J/kg °C.
items.random_wrong: ∆E in joules per second, and ∆θ in degrees Celsius, °C

items.q: A student uses ∆E = m c ∆θ for a 250 g block of aluminium. What should be substituted for m?
items.correct: 0.25, because the mass must be in kilograms
items.misconception: 250, because that is the mass given in the question
items.why: Grams are the everyday laboratory unit, and the substitution is done before the units are checked. Mass, m, in these equations is in kilograms. Divide a mass in grams by 1000 before substituting, or the answer comes out 1000 times too large.
items.random_wrong: 2.50, because grams are converted by dividing by 100

items.q: What are the units of specific heat capacity, and why does a temperature appear in them?
items.correct: J/kg °C, because the value fixes one kilogram and a one degree rise
items.misconception: J/kg, because the value is quoted for one kilogram of substance
items.why: The 'per kilogram' part is remembered from the word 'specific' and the temperature condition is dropped. The definition fixes both conditions: one kilogram and one degree Celsius. So the unit carries both, J/kg °C.
items.random_wrong: J/°C, because the value is quoted for one degree Celsius

items.q: Which statement is the specification definition of the specific heat capacity of a substance?
items.correct: The energy required to raise one kilogram of it by one degree Celsius
items.misconception: The energy required to raise the whole of the sample by one degree Celsius
items.why: The word 'specific' is not read as 'per kilogram', so the mass condition drops out of the definition. 'Specific' means per kilogram. The value is quoted for exactly one kilogram, which is why mass is multiplied in when ∆E = m c ∆θ is used.
items.random_wrong: The energy required to change the state of one kilogram of it

items.q: Blocks P and Q have the same mass. P has the higher specific heat capacity. The same energy is supplied to each block. What happens?
items.correct: Q has the greater temperature rise, needing less energy per °C
items.misconception: P has the greater temperature rise, because its capacity is larger
items.why: 'High capacity' is read as 'good at getting hot' rather than 'needs a lot of energy per degree'. A high specific heat capacity means more energy is needed per kilogram per degree Celsius, so for the same energy input the temperature rise is smaller.
items.random_wrong: Both rise by the same amount, since the energy supplied is equal

items.q: 10 500 J are supplied to 0.50 kg of water, which does not boil. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. What is the temperature change?
items.why: The word 'specific' is not read as 'per kilogram', so the mass condition drops out of the definition. 'Specific' means per kilogram. The value is quoted for exactly one kilogram, which is why mass is multiplied in when ∆E = m c ∆θ is used.

items.q: 10 kg of water is heated from 20 °C to 50 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. What is the change in thermal energy?
items.why: The word 'specific' is not read as 'per kilogram', so the mass condition drops out of the definition. 'Specific' means per kilogram. The value is quoted for exactly one kilogram, which is why mass is multiplied in when ∆E = m c ∆θ is used.

items.q: What is meant by the latent heat of a substance?
items.correct: The energy that is needed for a substance to change state
items.misconception: The energy stored by a substance once it has melted
items.why: Everyday speech treats heat as a fluid: 'let the heat out', 'the heat in the room', 'keep the heat in'. Heating is the transfer, not the store. What the object stores is internal energy, held by its own particles.
items.random_wrong: The energy needed to raise a substance by one degree

items.q: Steam is produced steadily from boiling water at 100 °C. What happens to the energy that is supplied?
items.correct: It changes the energy stored but not the temperature
items.misconception: It raises the temperature of the water past 100 °C
items.why: Energy in is linked directly to temperature out, with no separate store for the change of state. During a change of state the energy supplied goes into the potential energy store of the particles, separating them. The temperature stays constant until the change of state is complete.
items.random_wrong: It is stored in the heater until the boiling has finished

items.q: Which energy store of the particles increases while a solid melts at constant temperature?
items.correct: Their potential energy, as the particles are pulled apart
items.misconception: Their kinetic energy, because the particles must be moving faster
items.why: Energy in is equated with faster particles, which is the only mechanism most students have been shown. Faster particles would mean a higher temperature, and the temperature is constant during melting. The energy goes into the potential energy store instead.
items.random_wrong: Their thermal energy, as heat flows into the solid and is stored

items.q: Which statement is the specification definition of the specific latent heat of a substance?
items.correct: The energy to change the state of one kilogram with no temperature change
items.misconception: The energy needed to change the state of a whole sample of it
items.why: The word 'specific' is not read as 'per kilogram', so the mass condition drops out of the definition. 'Specific' means per kilogram. The value is quoted for exactly one kilogram, which is why mass is multiplied in when ∆E = m c ∆θ is used.
items.random_wrong: The energy needed to raise one kilogram of it by one degree Celsius

items.q: Which equation gives the energy needed for a change of state?
items.correct: energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat
items.misconception: energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat × ∆θ
items.why: ∆E = m c ∆θ is met first and is then used as the template for every thermal calculation. There is no temperature change during a change of state, so there is no ∆θ to include. The equation is simply E = m L.
items.random_wrong: energy for a state change = mass ÷ specific latent heat

items.q: The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 330 000 J/kg. How much energy is needed to melt 0.30 kg of ice that is already at 0 °C?
items.why: The word 'per' is read as an instruction to divide, and with a mass below one kilogram dividing gives a bigger number, which feels like the safer answer. 'Per kilogram' states the value for each kilogram, so for m kilograms you multiply by m. The same applies to specific heat capacity in ∆E = m c ∆θ.

items.q: In E = m L, which units does the specification give for the three quantities?
items.correct: E in joules, m in kilograms, L in joules per kilogram
items.misconception: E in joules, m in kilograms, L in joules per kilogram per °C
items.why: Both quantities are called 'specific', so the more familiar unit is carried across without checking what the quantity means. There is no temperature change during a change of state, so no 'per degree Celsius' appears. Specific latent heat is simply joules per kilogram.
items.random_wrong: E in joules, m in grams, L in joules per kilogram of substance

items.q: Which change of state does the specific latent heat of fusion describe?
items.correct: The change of state from a solid to a liquid, that is melting
items.misconception: The change of state from liquid to vapour, that is boiling
items.why: 'Fusion' sounds like intense heat (nuclear fusion, fusing metals), so it is attached to the hottest change of state a student can think of. Fusion here means melting: solid to liquid. Liquid to vapour is described by the specific latent heat of vaporisation.
items.random_wrong: The change of state from a solid straight to a vapour

items.q: Which change of state does the specific latent heat of vaporisation describe?
items.correct: The change of state from a liquid to a vapour
items.misconception: The change of state from a solid straight into a gas
items.why: 'Fusion' sounds like intense heat (nuclear fusion, fusing metals), so it is attached to the hottest change of state a student can think of. Fusion here means melting: solid to liquid. Liquid to vapour is described by the specific latent heat of vaporisation.
items.random_wrong: The change of state from solid to liquid

items.q: A solid is heated at a steady rate and a graph of temperature against time is plotted. What does a flat section of the graph show?
items.correct: The substance is changing state while energy is supplied
items.misconception: The substance has reached the hottest temperature it can ever reach
items.why: A horizontal line is read as 'no change at all' rather than 'no change in the quantity on the y-axis'. Only the temperature is unchanged. The substance is melting or boiling, and the length of the flat section shows how much energy that took.
items.random_wrong: The heater has been switched off, so no energy is transferred

items.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes specific heat capacity from specific latent heat?
items.correct: Specific heat capacity needs a temperature change; latent heat does not
items.misconception: They are two names for one quantity, so either may be used for any change
items.why: Both are 'specific' properties, both are quoted per kilogram, and both appear in similar-looking equations. Use c and ∆E = m c ∆θ when the temperature changes; use L and E = m L when the state changes at constant temperature.
items.random_wrong: Specific heat capacity changes state; specific latent heat changes temperature

items.q: Does the internal energy of a substance change while it is boiling?
items.correct: Yes. The energy supplied increases the internal energy even though the temperature is constant.
items.misconception: If the temperature is not changing then the internal energy is not changing either.
items.why: Internal energy and temperature are treated as the same quantity, so a steady thermometer reading is read as a steady energy store. Internal energy includes the potential energy of the particles. During a change of state that part rises while temperature, which tracks kinetic energy, stays the same.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.3.2 Internal energy and energy transfers
